questions.q: What is an OLTP system optimized for?
options: Running scheduled batch reports overnight
Storing every metric's definition in one governed place
Reading large amounts of aggregated historical data
Fast, safe writes of small, individual transactions
questions.explain: OLTP systems — order-entry apps, CRMs, billing systems — are normalized specifically to make individual inserts, updates, and deletes fast and consistent.

questions.q: Why does a normalized OLTP schema tend to be slow for a query like "revenue by region by quarter"?
options: OLTP tables don't support the SUM() function
OLTP systems physically cannot run SELECT queries
Normalized tables can only be queried once per day
Answering that question typically means joining many tables — every join costs real query time at scale
questions.explain: A fully normalized schema usually requires joining 8-10 tables to reconstruct an aggregate business answer, whereas a dimensional model answers the same question with a handful of joins.

questions.q: What's a real risk of running heavy analytical queries directly against a production OLTP database?
options: OLTP databases automatically delete old data to prevent this
There is no risk — OLTP and OLAP workloads are identical
The reporting queries can compete with and slow down the live application's transactions
SQL Server blocks all read queries against OLTP tables by design
questions.explain: A large analytical scan can contend for the same resources and locks the live transactional workload depends on, which is one of the concrete reasons warehouses exist as separate systems.

questions.q: Why doesn't a typical OLTP schema answer "which region did this order actually ship from, historically" well?
options: That kind of question is impossible to answer in any system
OLTP systems only store data for the current calendar year
OLTP systems don't store region information at all
OLTP tables usually hold only the current value of an attribute, not its history over time
questions.explain: An OLTP customer or order record typically reflects only the current state — tracking how an attribute's value looked at different points in time is exactly the problem Slowly Changing Dimensions (Chapters 3-4) are designed to solve.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does THIS course add beyond what T-SQL Development already introduced about warehousing?
options: How to actually design a dimensional model yourself — grain, fact types, dimension design, SCDs, staging, and physical build — not just recognize the vocabulary
Nothing — the two courses cover identical material
How to write basic SELECT statements
How to install SQL Server Management Studio
questions.explain: T-SQL Development's warehousing chapter was a vocabulary preview; this course is where dimensional modeling becomes a real, hands-on design skill, ending in a capstone that builds a physical warehouse.
